input.question: How is lead parts per million tested in soil?
input.ground_truth: There are several analytical tools one can use to determine the concentration of trace metals including [Atomic Absorption Spectroscopy (AAS)](_URL_3_) [Atomic Emission Spectroscopy (AES)](_URL_1_) [Mass Spectrometry](_URL_2_) It is commonplace for all of these methods to build 'calibration curves' using the [standard addition method](_URL_0_), or by some other methods.

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine the soil is like a big jar of peanut butter. If we want to know if there is a tiny bit of something called "lead" mixed in, we can't see it with our eyes because it's so, so small.

Scientists use a special way to check. They take a little bit of the soil and put it in a science machine. This machine is like a super detective. It can smell or find the tiny lead pieces, even if there are only a few in a million tiny pieces of soil.

They count how many lead pieces are in that little bit and then use math to figure out how many lead pieces are in the whole jar (the whole soil). That's how we know how much lead is in the soil, measured in "parts per million," which means how many tiny pieces of lead are in one million tiny pieces of soil.

So, they use a special machine to find the tiny lead pieces in the soil!
